about: Ranked topic backlog for toon long-form videos (Mon/Wed/Fri) and their short angles. The weekly automation takes the highest-ranked topic with status 'queued' per format, then marks it 'used' with the week id. Short angles are leads only: every fact is checked against sources before a script is written.
research_notes: WHAT PERFORMS: (1) 'ENTIRE History of X' is the single strongest long-form format right now. Historically's 'The ENTIRE History of ROME' hit 7.5M views in 4 months (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EHLI2WZUtXs) and its 'ENTIRE History of CHINA' passed 4.1M in 3 weeks. Animated History's Germany did 557K in 2 weeks and Poland 1.1M (https://www.youtube.com/@AnimatedHistoryy). Rome, China, Egypt, Mongols and Japan lead the Monday list because demand is proven even where others have covered them. (2) Serious History's list format works best when superlative plus emotional: 'Most Epic Deaths in History' 6.3M, 'Extreme Vigilante Justice' 6.9M, 'Craziest 1v1 Fights' 3.1M, 'Most Epic Revenge Stories' 2.6M, 'Craziest CRASHOUTS' 535K in a month, 'The HUMILIATING Death of the Richest Man in Rome' 1.2M (https://www.youtube.com/@SeriousHistory). OverSimplified proves absurd-small-war and royal-drama topics at scale: WW2 Pt1 101M, Henry VIII 47.9M, The Pig War 38.7M (https://creatordb.app/creatorstats/oversimplified/). TED-Ed's Mansa Musa has 8.9M, which makes the richest-person angle the strongest Friday hook. RPM: finance/business CPM is about $10–45 with RPM about $5–20 (https://vloggingpro.com/youtube-cpm/); education CPM is about $10–25 with RPM about $2.75–6.88 (https://www.lenostube.com/en/youtube-cpm-rpm-rates/). Faceless history long-form earns about $4–9 RPM, but history Shorts only about $0.10–0.25 RPM, so Shorts are for discovery (https://www.autoclips.app/faceless-history-channel). Q4 CPMs are the highest of the year and January the lowest; videos over 8 minutes with mid-rolls earn 2–3x more. The 12–16 minute length is ideal. Finance topics (Friday) should carry finance keywords in titles (crash, bubble, richest, money, bankrupt) to attract finance advertisers. SAFETY: gore (sacrifice, executions) is kept off-camera. Modern entries stop before 1991 or earlier (Korea to 1910, China to 1912, USA to 1969). No living politicians and no Holocaust comedy. The Rothschilds are deliberately excluded because of conspiracy-theory adjacency. Every short labelled 'legend' or 'reported' must keep that qualifier in narration, and every short must still go through the fact-check pass before narration.

monday.title: The ENTIRE History of Rome in 10 Minutes
monday.subject: Rome
monday.why: Biggest proven demand in the genre: Historically's 'The ENTIRE History of ROME' passed 7.5M views in 4 months. Endless comedic material (emperors, gladiators, toga politics).
shorts: Emperor Vespasian taxed public urine (used by launderers) and told his son money doesn't stink: 'pecunia non olet'.
In 193 AD the Praetorian Guard auctioned the whole empire; Didius Julianus won and was killed 66 days later.
Pirates kidnapped young Julius Caesar; he demanded they raise his ransom from 20 to 50 talents, then came back and executed them (Plutarch).
Emperor Commodus fought as a gladiator in the arena and billed the treasury for each appearance (Cassius Dio).
Roman concrete has lasted 2,000 years; the Pantheon is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome on Earth.
Ancient Rome hit roughly a million people; no European city matched that until London around 1800.
Caligula's plan to make his horse Incitatus a consul comes from ancient gossip writers; treat it as a rumour, not a fact (legend).
Rome's founding by twins raised by a wolf in 753 BC is a legend; Romans themselves argued about it.

monday.title: The ENTIRE History of China in 10 Minutes
monday.subject: China
monday.why: Historically's 'ENTIRE History of CHINA' hit 2.2M in 5 days and 4.1M in 3 weeks; the brief cites Animated History's China at 759K. Stop the story in 1912 to avoid modern politics.
shorts: China's first emperor Qin Shi Huang probably died from mercury pills he took to become immortal.
The Terracotta Army has around 8,000 clay soldiers, and no two faces were made exactly alike.
Gunpowder was discovered by Chinese alchemists who were looking for an elixir of eternal life.
China's imperial civil-service exams ran for about 1,300 years, from 605 until 1905.
Song-dynasty China issued the world's first government paper money in the 11th century.
Admiral Zheng He sailed to East Africa and brought a live giraffe back to the Ming emperor in 1414.
Wu Zetian is the only woman in Chinese history to rule as emperor in her own right.
You cannot see the Great Wall from the Moon with the naked eye; that one is a myth.

monday.title: The ENTIRE History of Ancient Egypt in 10 Minutes
monday.subject: Ancient Egypt
monday.why: Evergreen top-searched civilization; pyramids and mummies are instantly visual. Strong with all ages and very advertiser-safe.
shorts: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.
The pyramid builders were paid workers who got bread and beer rations. They were not slaves.
Around 1157 BC, tomb workers at Deir el-Medina staged the first recorded labour strike in history over late wages.
The Great Pyramid was the tallest human-made structure on Earth for about 3,800 years.
Cleopatra was of Macedonian Greek descent, and she was the first of her dynasty to learn Egyptian.
For centuries Europeans ground up Egyptian mummies and sold the powder as medicine, called 'mumia'.
Tutankhamun was only about 19 when he died; his tomb was found almost intact in 1922.
A pharaoh smearing honey on servants to keep flies off himself is a later tale (legend).

monday.title: The ENTIRE History of the Mongol Empire in 10 Minutes
monday.subject: Mongol Empire
monday.why: Largest land empire ever; Genghis Khan is one of the most-searched historical figures. It has horses, arrows and chaos, all easy to animate.
shorts: At its peak the Mongol Empire covered about 24 million km², the largest contiguous land empire ever.
The Mongol 'Yam' was a network of relay stations with fresh horses spread across the empire, like a medieval pony express.
Europe was saved in 1241 partly because Great Khan Ögedei died and the Mongol commanders rode home to pick a successor.
Typhoons wrecked Kublai Khan's fleets invading Japan in 1274 and 1281; the Japanese called them 'kamikaze' (divine winds).
The Mongols exempted clergy of many religions from taxes, which was unusually tolerant for the era.
Nobody knows where Genghis Khan is buried; the site is still undiscovered.
A 2003 genetic study suggested about 0.5% of men worldwide share one lineage possibly linked to Genghis Khan's family.
Marco Polo wrote that Mongol riders could survive long rides by drinking their horses' blood (reported by Polo).

monday.title: The ENTIRE History of Japan in 10 Minutes
monday.subject: Japan
monday.why: Samurai, shoguns and ninjas carry huge anime-adjacent demand; bill wurtz's 'history of japan' has 86M views. Stop at 1945 and frame WWII carefully.
shorts: Kongō Gumi, a Japanese temple-building company founded in 578 AD, ran independently for over 1,400 years until 2006.
Yasuke, an African man, served the warlord Oda Nobunaga in the 1580s and was given samurai status.
Japan almost completely sealed itself off from the world for over 200 years (about 1639 to 1853).
In 1876 Japan banned samurai from carrying swords in public, which ended an era overnight.
Hiroo Onoda kept fighting WWII in the Philippine jungle until 1974 because nobody officially ordered him to stop.
Japan's imperial family is considered the oldest continuous hereditary monarchy in the world.
Two typhoons helped destroy Mongol invasion fleets in 1274 and 1281.
The earliest emperors, such as Jimmu in 660 BC, are legendary rather than historical figures (legend).

monday.title: The ENTIRE History of the Ottoman Empire in 10 Minutes
monday.subject: Ottoman Empire
monday.why: It lasted more than 600 years across three continents, with high search demand from Europe, the Middle East and the US. Palace intrigue and sultans make natural characters.
shorts: The Ottoman Empire lasted over 600 years, from 1299 to 1922.
Janissary ranks were named after kitchen jobs, and flipping over their soup cauldrons was the signal for revolt.
Sultan Murad IV banned coffee and tobacco and was said to prowl Istanbul in disguise to catch offenders.
Ottoman princes were often confined for years in a palace apartment nicknamed 'the Cage' (Kafes).
The 'Tulip Era' (1718–1730) was named after an Ottoman elite craze for tulips.
Suleiman the Magnificent reigned for 46 years, the longest of any Ottoman sultan.
In the 1600s sultans' mothers held so much power that historians call it the 'Sultanate of Women'.

monday.title: The ENTIRE History of the Vikings in 10 Minutes
monday.subject: Vikings
monday.why: Viking content is evergreen (shows, games, memes), is naturally funny and is very visual. Mostly advertiser-safe when the raids aren't played for gore.
shorts: Vikings almost certainly never wore horned helmets; the look comes from 19th-century opera costumes.
Leif Erikson reached North America around 1000 AD, about 500 years before Columbus (L'Anse aux Meadows).
Viking graffiti carved in runes can still be seen in the Hagia Sophia in Istanbul.
Bluetooth technology is named after the Viking king Harald 'Bluetooth' Gormsson.
The Icelandic word for Saturday, 'laugardagur', means 'washing day'.
The Viking Age is often said to end in 1066, when Harald Hardrada died at Stamford Bridge.
Ragnar Lothbrok is at least partly legendary; historians debate whether he existed (legend).
Erik the Red named Greenland 'green' so that people would want to move there, according to the Icelandic sagas.

monday.title: The ENTIRE History of Britain in 10 Minutes
monday.subject: Britain
monday.why: Huge UK and US search demand and top-tier CPM countries. OverSimplified's Henry VIII has 47.9M views.
shorts: The Anglo-Zanzibar War of 1896 lasted about 38 to 45 minutes, the shortest war on record.
Stonehenge was begun around 3000 BC, centuries before the Great Pyramid.
Oliver Cromwell's head was displayed on a spike for about 20 years and was only buried in 1960.
The Great Fire of London in 1666 officially recorded only six deaths.
The 1858 'Great Stink' of the Thames was so bad that Parliament finally paid for London's sewers.
In 1920 the British Empire covered about a quarter of the world's land.
Henry VIII had six wives; the rhyme is 'divorced, beheaded, died, divorced, beheaded, survived'.

monday.title: The ENTIRE History of Ancient Greece in 10 Minutes
monday.subject: Ancient Greece
monday.why: Evergreen school-curriculum topic with steady search. Philosophers and Spartans make great comedy characters.
shorts: The Greek word 'idiotes' originally meant a private citizen who stayed out of public affairs.
Draco's laws were so harsh that they gave us the word 'draconian'.
Diogenes lived in a large jar and reportedly told Alexander the Great to stop blocking his sunlight.
The Antikythera mechanism, made around 100 BC, is a hand-cranked astronomical calculator.
Ancient Olympic athletes competed completely naked.
Socrates was sentenced to death by a jury in 399 BC and drank hemlock.
Pheidippides running from Marathon to Athens and then dropping dead is a later legend (legend).
Aeschylus being killed by a tortoise dropped by an eagle is an ancient story (legend).

monday.title: The ENTIRE History of France in 10 Minutes
monday.subject: France
monday.why: Napoleon, Versailles and the Revolution are all top-searched, with strong tier-1 audience interest.
shorts: Louis XIV reigned for 72 years and 110 days, the longest reign of any major European monarch.
Napoleon was about 5'7", average for his time; the 'short' myth came partly from French inches and British cartoons.
The Hundred Years' War actually lasted 116 years (1337–1453).
France last used the guillotine for an execution in 1977.
The Eiffel Tower was built for the 1889 World's Fair with a permit to stand for only 20 years.
Joan of Arc was about 17 when she led a French army to lift the siege of Orléans.
Charlemagne tried to learn to write late in life and kept tablets under his pillow, but mostly failed (Einhard).

monday.title: The ENTIRE History of Russia in 10 Minutes (862–1991)
monday.subject: Russia (pre-1991)
monday.why: High global search demand. Tsars, Peter the Great and the space race are rich material; the story stops at 1991 to avoid the current conflict.
shorts: Peter the Great taxed beards; payers got a token saying 'the beard is a superfluous burden'.
Russia sold Alaska to the USA in 1867 for $7.2 million, about 2 cents an acre.
Russia's 'October Revolution' happened in November by the modern calendar; Russia still used the Julian calendar.
Catherine the Great wasn't Russian; she was born a German princess, Sophie of Anhalt-Zerbst.
The Soviet Tsar Bomba (1961) is the most powerful explosive ever detonated.
Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space on April 12, 1961.
'Potemkin villages' (fake towns built to impress Catherine) are mostly exaggerated (legend).

monday.title: The ENTIRE History of the Persian Empire in 10 Minutes
monday.subject: Persia
monday.why: Persia is under-covered compared with Rome, has strong search demand and a massive Middle East and diaspora audience. It is the counterpoint to 300.
shorts: Herodotus described Persian royal couriers as stopped by neither snow nor rain; the line is carved on New York's main post office.
Xerxes reportedly had the Hellespont whipped 300 times after a storm wrecked his bridge (Herodotus).
The Persian 'Immortals' were an elite unit that was always kept at exactly 10,000 men.
Persians built 'yakhchāl' ice houses that stored ice through desert summers.
Persepolis work records show paid workers, including extra rations for women who had just given birth.
Alexander the Great burned Persepolis in 330 BC.
Cambyses' army of 50,000 vanishing in a sandstorm comes from Herodotus (legend).

monday.title: The ENTIRE History of the Aztec Empire in 10 Minutes
monday.subject: Aztecs
monday.why: Big US and Mexico search demand and a visually spectacular floating city. Keep human sacrifice off-camera to stay advertiser-safe.
shorts: Tenochtitlan was built on an island in a lake and had perhaps 200,000 people, more than most European cities.
The Aztecs used cacao beans as money, and people counterfeited them.
Aztec farmers grew food on 'chinampas', artificial islands in the lake.
Aztec education was compulsory for boys of all classes.
Cortés arrived with about 500 Spaniards; tens of thousands of Indigenous allies did most of the fighting.
Bernal Díaz wrote that Moctezuma was served around 50 jugs of frothy chocolate.
Mexico's flag shows the legend of an eagle on a cactus marking where to found Tenochtitlan (legend).

monday.title: The ENTIRE History of the United States in 10 Minutes
monday.subject: USA
monday.why: The US is the highest-RPM audience with enormous search demand. Stop before recent decades and avoid living politicians.
shorts: The Pilgrims' own journal says they landed at Plymouth partly because they were running out of beer.
Most of the Declaration of Independence was signed on August 2, 1776, not July 4.
John Adams and Thomas Jefferson both died on July 4, 1826, the 50th anniversary of the Declaration.
The British burned the White House in 1814.
The Louisiana Purchase cost about 3 cents an acre and doubled the size of the USA.
Abraham Lincoln is the only US president with a patent: a device to lift boats over shoals.
In 1919 a wave of molasses flooded Boston's North End and killed 21 people.

monday.title: The ENTIRE History of Spain in 10 Minutes
monday.subject: Spain
monday.why: Global empire story with big US, LatAm and Europe demand; This Is History's 'Entire History of Spain' has 656K views.
shorts: The Reconquista lasted about 781 years, from 711 to 1492.
Philip II of Spain ruled a global empire yet defaulted on his debts four times.
The Spanish silver dollar ('piece of eight') was legal tender in the USA until 1857.
Charles II of Spain was so affected by royal inbreeding that he was nicknamed 'the Bewitched'.
The Philippines are named after King Philip II.
The 1918 'Spanish flu' did not start in Spain; neutral Spain simply reported it openly.
El Cid's corpse being tied to his horse to scare the enemy is a legend (legend).

monday.title: The ENTIRE History of the Byzantine Empire in 10 Minutes
monday.subject: Byzantine Empire
monday.why: Rome's forgotten second half has 1,000 years of absurd palace drama. It is a distinct topic from the already-done fall of Constantinople.
shorts: The Byzantines never called themselves Byzantine; they called themselves Romans.
The recipe for 'Greek fire', a weapon that burned on water, has been lost.
In 532, chariot-racing fan clubs started the Nika riots, which nearly toppled Emperor Justinian.
Monks smuggled silkworm eggs out of China in hollow canes around 552, starting Byzantine silk production.
Hagia Sophia was the world's largest cathedral for almost 1,000 years.
Empress Theodora rose from a stage performer to co-ruler of the empire.
Justinian II had his nose cut off, came back and retook the throne; some sources say he wore a golden nose.
'Born in the purple' comes from a purple-stone room where Byzantine royal babies were born.

monday.title: The ENTIRE History of the Mughal Empire in 10 Minutes
monday.subject: Mughal India
monday.why: A massive Indian and diaspora audience; the Taj Mahal and the Koh-i-Noor are huge hooks. Keep the religious framing neutral.
shorts: Around 1700 Mughal India produced about a quarter of the world's economic output (Maddison estimate).
Babur, the first Mughal emperor, was descended from both Timur and Genghis Khan.
Emperor Akbar probably could not read, yet he built a library of about 24,000 manuscripts.
The Taj Mahal took about 20,000 workers and roughly 20 years to build.
In 1739 the Persian ruler Nader Shah carried off the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor diamond.
Emperor Humayun died after falling down the stairs of his library.
Jahangir hung a 'chain of justice' with bells that any subject could ring to ask for his help (reported).

monday.title: The ENTIRE History of the Inca Empire in 10 Minutes
monday.subject: Inca
monday.why: A mystery empire with no writing and no money makes a strong curiosity hook, and Machu Picchu is a visual icon.
shorts: The Inca ran a huge empire with no money and no markets; taxes were paid in labour.
The Inca recorded information with 'quipu', knotted strings.
The Inca road network stretched about 40,000 km.
Relay runners called 'chasquis' could carry messages about 240 km a day.
Inca surgeons performed skull surgery, and most patients survived.
Pizarro captured Emperor Atahualpa with about 168 men; Atahualpa offered to fill a room with gold.
Machu Picchu became world-famous only after Hiram Bingham publicised it in 1911.

monday.title: The ENTIRE History of the Holy Roman Empire in 10 Minutes
monday.subject: Holy Roman Empire
monday.why: The topic comes with a famous built-in joke (neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire), and German and European history is proven (Animated History's Germany: 557K).
shorts: Voltaire joked the Holy Roman Empire was 'neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire'.
The empire was a patchwork of hundreds of separate states.
Emperors were elected by seven 'prince-electors' under the Golden Bull of 1356.
In 1618 officials thrown out of a Prague castle window survived the fall, helping spark the Thirty Years' War.
Charles V ruled so much land that the sun literally never set on his realms.
Napoleon effectively ended the 1,000-year empire in 1806.
Legend says Emperor Frederick Barbarossa sleeps inside a mountain waiting to return (legend).

monday.title: The ENTIRE History of the Mali Empire in 10 Minutes
monday.subject: Mali Empire
monday.why: Under-served African history with strong demand (TED-Ed's Mansa Musa: 8.9M). It bridges to the Friday money content.
shorts: The Mali Empire was founded by Sundiata Keita, whose story is told in the Epic of Sundiata.
Mansa Musa's 1324 pilgrimage handed out so much gold that its value in Cairo stayed depressed for years (al-Umari).
The 1375 Catalan Atlas shows Mansa Musa holding a gold nugget.
Timbuktu became a centre of learning with hundreds of thousands of manuscripts.
The Djinguereber mosque in Timbuktu, built in 1327, is made of mud and is still standing.
Ibn Battuta visited Mali in 1352 and wrote about it.
Musa said his predecessor Abu Bakr II sailed into the Atlantic with a huge fleet and never came back (legend).

monday.title: The ENTIRE History of the Maya in 10 Minutes
monday.subject: Maya
monday.why: Pyramids, astronomy and the 2012 myth make a strong mystery hook with high US search.
shorts: The Maya developed a symbol for zero independently of the Old World.
The last independent Maya kingdom, Nojpetén, held out until 1697.
Millions of Maya people live today, and many still speak Mayan languages.
The Maya calendar never predicted the world would end in 2012.
'Maya blue' pigment is so durable that it survives on murals centuries later.
At the equinox, shadows at Chichén Itzá form the shape of a serpent sliding down the pyramid.
The Maya played a ball game with a heavy solid-rubber ball and scored by getting it through stone rings on the walls.
The Maya drank cacao as a frothy drink long before Europeans knew chocolate.

monday.title: The ENTIRE History of Carthage in 10 Minutes
monday.subject: Carthage
monday.why: Hannibal and his elephants are a top hook, and a rivalry story against Rome brings in the Rome audience.
shorts: Carthage's military harbour was a ring-shaped basin that could hold about 220 warships.
Rome built its first real navy by copying a wrecked Carthaginian warship (Polybius).
Hannibal crossed the Alps with war elephants in 218 BC.
At Cannae in 216 BC, Hannibal's army destroyed a Roman army of about 80,000 in a single day.
Rome 'salting the earth' of Carthage is a myth invented in modern times.
The Roman Senate ordered a Carthaginian farming manual by Mago translated into Latin.
Queen Dido tricking a local king with an ox hide to found Carthage is a legend (legend).

monday.title: The ENTIRE History of Mesopotamia in 10 Minutes
monday.subject: Mesopotamia/Sumer
monday.why: The 'firsts' hook (first writing, laws, beer, customer complaint) is extremely shareable.
shorts: The oldest known customer complaint (about 1750 BC) is from Nanni, angry that Ea-nasir sold him bad copper.
Mesopotamians invented one of the first writing systems, cuneiform, originally to track grain and beer.
Our 60-minute hour comes from Babylonian base-60 maths.
The Code of Hammurabi lists 282 laws carved on a stone pillar.
The Epic of Gilgamesh is one of the oldest surviving works of literature.
Workers in Mesopotamia were often paid in beer and bread.
The Hanging Gardens of Babylon may not have existed in Babylon at all (legend).

monday.title: The ENTIRE History of Korea in 10 Minutes (to 1910)
monday.subject: Korea
monday.why: A big K-culture-driven audience. Stop at 1910 to avoid modern North/South politics.
shorts: The oldest surviving book printed with metal movable type (Jikji, 1377) is Korean, 78 years before Gutenberg's Bible.
King Sejong's scholars created the Korean alphabet Hangul in 1443 so that ordinary people could read.
Admiral Yi Sun-sin won the Battle of Myeongnyang in 1597 with 13 ships against more than 100.
The Joseon dynasty lasted 518 years (1392–1910).
The name 'Korea' comes from the Goryeo dynasty.
Early kimchi wasn't red; chili peppers only reached Korea around the late 1500s.
The Silla kingdom was ruled by queens, including Queen Seondeok in the 600s.

monday.title: The ENTIRE History of Venice in 10 Minutes
monday.subject: Venice
monday.why: A money-and-power city (it links to the Friday format) and a visually unique floating city.
shorts: Venice is built on millions of wooden piles driven into the lagoon mud.
The Venetian Arsenal reportedly built a whole galley in a single day to impress King Henry III in 1574.
The Doge was elected through about 10 rounds that alternated random lottery draws with votes.
The word 'quarantine' comes from the Venetian 'quaranta giorni', meaning 40 days.
Venetian glassmakers were banned from leaving the Republic to protect trade secrets.
The Republic of Venice lasted about 1,100 years until Napoleon ended it in 1797.
Venetian merchants reportedly smuggled St Mark's body out of Alexandria in 828 under pork (legend).

monday.title: The ENTIRE History of Ethiopia in 10 Minutes
monday.subject: Ethiopia
monday.why: An under-served topic (a small channel's 'Ethiopia in 14 Minutes' exists but has weak competition), with strong African diaspora interest and plenty of unique facts.
shorts: Ethiopia defeated an Italian invasion at the Battle of Adwa in 1896.
Ethiopia's calendar has 13 months and runs about 7 to 8 years behind the Gregorian calendar.
The Kingdom of Aksum was minting its own coins around 270 AD.
The churches of Lalibela were carved downward out of solid rock around the 1200s.
The fossil 'Lucy', 3.2 million years old, was found in Ethiopia in 1974.
The story of a goatherd named Kaldi discovering coffee from dancing goats is a legend (legend).
Ethiopian tradition says the Ark of the Covenant is kept in a chapel in Aksum (legend/claim).

monday.title: The ENTIRE History of Scotland in 10 Minutes
monday.subject: Scotland
monday.why: UK tier-1 audience; Braveheart myths make easy comedy.
shorts: Scotland's national animal is the unicorn.
In 1457 King James II of Scotland banned golf because it distracted men from archery practice.
In 1603 Scotland's King James VI also became King of England.
The Darien scheme lost a huge share of Scotland's capital and helped push it into the 1707 union.
Scottish students stole the Stone of Destiny from Westminster Abbey on Christmas 1950.
The Romans built two walls in Britain: Hadrian's and the Antonine Wall in Scotland.
Robert the Bruce being inspired by a persistent spider is a legend (legend).

wednesday.title: The Weirdest Deaths in History
wednesday.subject: Bizarre deaths
wednesday.why: Proven format: Serious History 'Most Epic Deaths in History' 6.3M plus part 2 at 1.7M. Played for absurdity, not gore.
shorts: Greek King Alexander died in 1920 from an infection after a pet monkey bit him.
Swedish King Adolf Frederick died in 1771 after a huge feast reportedly finished with 14 servings of semla buns.
Mughal Emperor Humayun died after falling down the stairs of his library in 1556.
Lawyer Clement Vallandigham accidentally shot himself in 1871 while showing a court how the victim might have done it.
An ancient account says Attila the Hun died of a nosebleed on his wedding night in 453.
Tycho Brahe supposedly died because he was too polite to leave a banquet to pee (Kepler's account; later disputed).
Emperor Frederick Barbarossa drowned crossing a river on the way to the Crusade in 1190.
Aeschylus being killed by a tortoise dropped by an eagle is an ancient story (legend).

wednesday.title: The Most Ridiculous Wars in History
wednesday.subject: Absurd wars
wednesday.why: Very high comedy value; OverSimplified's Pig War has 38.7M views.
shorts: The 1859 Pig War between the USA and Britain had one casualty: a pig.
The Anglo-Zanzibar War of 1896 lasted about 38 to 45 minutes.
In the 1784 'Kettle War' the only shot fired reportedly hit a soup kettle.
In 1325 Modena and Bologna fought a battle; Modena's captured trophy, a wooden bucket, is still displayed there.
The 'War of Jenkins' Ear' (1739) was named after a British captain whose ear was cut off by Spanish coast guards.
In 1932 Australian soldiers with machine guns fought emus, and the emus won.
The '335-year war' between the Isles of Scilly and the Netherlands probably never officially existed (legend).

wednesday.title: The Craziest Things Genghis Khan Did
wednesday.subject: Genghis Khan
wednesday.why: It mirrors Serious History's 'Craziest Things Alexander the Great Did' at 1.5M, and Genghis is among the most-searched conquerors.
shorts: Genghis Khan was born Temüjin; 'Genghis Khan' was a title he took in 1206.
As a teenager he killed his own half-brother in a dispute over food.
He was once captured and locked in a wooden neck yoke, and he escaped.
An enemy archer shot his horse; Genghis hired him and named him Jebe ('arrow'). He became a top general.
When the Khwarazmian Empire killed his envoys around 1219, Genghis wiped the empire off the map.
He promoted people on merit rather than noble birth, which was radical for the time.
Stories that his burial workers were killed to hide his tomb are legend (legend).

wednesday.title: The Most Badass Women in History
wednesday.subject: Women warriors and rulers
wednesday.why: Broad appeal across demographics, advertiser-friendly and packed with strong characters.
shorts: Ching Shih commanded a pirate fleet of tens of thousands, then negotiated a pardon and kept her loot.
Queen Nzinga of Ndongo, refused a chair by the Portuguese, reportedly sat on a servant's back to negotiate as an equal.
Mongol princess Khutulun reportedly challenged suitors to wrestle her for horses and won thousands (Marco Polo).
Queen Artemisia fought for Persia at Salamis; Xerxes reportedly said his men had become women and his women men.
Boudica led a revolt that burned Roman London around 60 AD.
Soviet sniper Lyudmila Pavlichenko was credited with 309 kills in WWII.
Joan of Arc led the French army at about 17.
Samurai woman Tomoe Gozen appears in the Tale of the Heike; she may be partly legendary (legend).

wednesday.title: The Dumbest Military Blunders in History
wednesday.subject: Military blunders
wednesday.why: Stupidity sells: 'Idiot Mistakes That Changed History'-type titles perform. Easy slapstick for stick figures.
shorts: In 1943, 34,000 Allied troops invaded Kiska island, whose Japanese garrison had left weeks earlier, and still took over 300 casualties.
Australia's 1932 Emu War: soldiers fired thousands of rounds and the emus came out ahead.
The Charge of the Light Brigade (1854) happened because of a garbled order.
Napoleon invaded Russia in 1812 with about 600,000 men; only a small fraction made it back.
In 1940 Germany went around France's Maginot Line through the Ardennes forest.
Crassus marched into the desert at Carrhae in 53 BC and lost about 20,000 men to horse archers.
The Austrian army 'fighting itself' at Karánsebes in 1788 is from later, possibly exaggerated accounts (legend).

wednesday.title: The Craziest Pirates in History
wednesday.subject: Pirates
wednesday.why: Evergreen, family-friendly adventure; Historically's 'That Time PIRATES started a COUNTRY' has 2.1M.
shorts: Stede Bonnet was a rich landowner with no sailing experience who bought a ship and became a pirate.
Henry Morgan went from pirate to knight and Lieutenant Governor of Jamaica.
Bartholomew 'Black Bart' Roberts captured around 400 ships and reportedly preferred tea to rum.
Pirate codes paid set compensation for injuries, such as losing an arm: an early form of insurance.
Blackbeard reportedly tucked slow-burning fuses under his hat to look terrifying in battle.
Ching Shih retired from piracy with a pardon and ran a gambling house.
Walking the plank was very rare; most of it is legend (legend).

wednesday.title: The Weirdest Roman Emperors
wednesday.subject: Roman emperors
wednesday.why: Rome is the top topic and emperor chaos is peak comedy. Keep it PG.
shorts: Commodus fought as a gladiator and charged Rome for every appearance (Cassius Dio).
Didius Julianus literally bought the empire at auction in 193 AD.
Caracalla granted citizenship to nearly all free men in the empire in 212 AD, partly to tax them (Cassius Dio).
Nero couldn't have 'fiddled while Rome burned'; the fiddle didn't exist yet, and he was reportedly away at Antium.
Ancient writers claim Caligula made soldiers collect seashells as 'spoils' from the sea (reported).
Elagabalus smothering dinner guests with rose petals comes from an unreliable source (legend).
The idea of Caligula making his horse a consul is ancient gossip (legend).

wednesday.title: The Craziest Things Julius Caesar Did
wednesday.subject: Julius Caesar
wednesday.why: One man, many insane moments; a proven 'Craziest Things X Did' format.
shorts: Kidnapped by pirates, Caesar insisted his ransom be raised from 20 to 50 talents (Plutarch).
His army built a bridge across the Rhine in about 10 days, crossed, then tore it down.
At Alesia he built a wall around the enemy town and a second wall facing outward against the relief army.
Fixing the calendar made 46 BC a 445-day year, the 'year of confusion'.
He wrote his war memoirs about himself in the third person.
'Et tu, Brute?' was written by Shakespeare; Suetonius reports he may have said 'You too, child?' in Greek.
The Caesarean section is almost certainly not named after his birth (legend).

wednesday.title: The Most Insane Kings and Queens in History
wednesday.subject: Mad monarchs
wednesday.why: Serious History 'Craziest CRASHOUTS in History' got 535K in a month. Royals behaving badly is safe comedy.
shorts: King Charles VI of France believed he was made of glass and feared he would shatter.
Joshua Norton declared himself 'Emperor of the United States' in 1859, and San Francisco shops accepted his homemade money.
Ludwig II of Bavaria nearly bankrupted himself building fairytale castles like Neuschwanstein.
Philip V of Spain had the singer Farinelli perform for him night after night for years.
Peter the Great loved dentistry and personally pulled his courtiers' teeth.
Joanna of Castile, 'Juana la Loca', reportedly travelled for months with her husband's coffin.
George III talking to an oak tree thinking it was the King of Prussia is a popular story (legend).

wednesday.title: The Most Epic Revenge Stories in History
wednesday.subject: Revenge
wednesday.why: Serious History 'Most Epic Revenge Stories' 2.6M and 'MORE Extreme Revenge' 2M. Framed as cleverness, not gore.
shorts: The 47 Ronin waited nearly two years to avenge their master in 1703, then turned themselves in.
After the French executed her husband, Jeanne de Clisson became a pirate with ships painted black (the 'Lioness of Brittany').
Caesar promised the pirates who kidnapped him he'd come back for them, and he did.
Genghis Khan destroyed an entire empire after its governor killed his merchants and envoys.
Hannibal reportedly swore eternal hatred of Rome at age 9 and spent his life keeping the oath (Polybius).
Olga of Kiev's elaborate revenge on the Drevlians comes from the Primary Chronicle, partly legendary (legend).
Queen Boudica's revolt against Rome began after Roman officials seized her family's lands and mistreated her family (Tacitus).

wednesday.title: The Craziest Things Napoleon Did
wednesday.subject: Napoleon
wednesday.why: Napoleon is one of the most-searched people in history, with endless meme potential.
shorts: Napoleon took about 167 scientists and scholars with his army to invade Egypt.
His expedition found the Rosetta Stone in 1799.
At his 1804 coronation he placed the crown on his own head.
Escaping Elba in 1815, he walked up to the troops sent to arrest him, and they joined him instead.
A memoir says a hunt organised for Napoleon ended with him chased off by a horde of tame rabbits (reported).
He wrote a romance novella, 'Clisson et Eugénie'.
The Napoleonic Code still shapes the laws of many countries today.

wednesday.title: The Most Genius Military Tricks in History
wednesday.subject: Military deception
wednesday.why: Clever-trick stories are highly watchable and brand-safe, with strong WWII interest.
shorts: Operation Mincemeat (1943): British spies planted fake invasion plans on a corpse and fooled Hitler.
The WWII 'Ghost Army' used inflatable tanks and fake radio chatter to fool the Germans.
Hannibal tied torches to cattle horns at night to trick a Roman army and slip out of a trap (217 BC).
Themistocles sent a fake traitor message to lure Xerxes into battle at Salamis (Herodotus).
WWI 'dazzle' camouflage painted ships in crazy stripes to confuse submarine aim.
Zhuge Liang 'borrowing' 100,000 arrows using straw boats comes from a novel (legend).
The Trojan Horse is a legend from Greek myth (legend).

wednesday.title: The Greatest Escapes in History
wednesday.subject: Escapes
wednesday.why: Heist-like tension, very family-friendly, with broad appeal.
shorts: In 1962 three men escaped Alcatraz using papier-mâché dummy heads and a raincoat raft; they were never found.
Hugo Grotius escaped a Dutch prison in 1621 hidden inside a book chest.
In 1849 Henry 'Box' Brown mailed himself to freedom in a wooden crate.
Casanova broke out of Venice's 'Leads' prison through the roof in 1756.
After losing the Battle of Worcester in 1651, future King Charles II hid in an oak tree.
76 POWs escaped in WWII's 'Great Escape' in 1944; only three made it home.
British POWs at Colditz built a glider out of bed slats and sheets.

wednesday.title: The Luckiest People in History
wednesday.subject: Luck and survival
wednesday.why: An uplifting, shareable twist on 'deaths' that works for all ages.
shorts: Tsutomu Yamaguchi survived both the Hiroshima and Nagasaki atomic bombs.
Violet Jessop was aboard the Olympic when it collided, then survived the Titanic and the Britannic sinkings.
Park ranger Roy Sullivan was struck by lightning seven times and survived.
Flight attendant Vesna Vulović survived a fall of about 10,000 m in 1972.
Juliane Koepcke fell about 3 km from a plane into the Amazon in 1971 and walked out after 11 days.
Titanic baker Charles Joughin survived hours in freezing water; he said he'd been drinking whisky.
Frane Selak, 'the world's luckiest man', has stories that can't be verified (legend).

wednesday.title: The Weirdest Crusades in History
wednesday.subject: Crusades
wednesday.why: Serious History's 'Most Disturbing Crusades' did 1.2M. Reframed toward absurd rather than disturbing to stay advertiser-safe.
shorts: The Fourth Crusade never reached the Holy Land; it sacked the Christian city of Constantinople in 1204.
A chronicler says some People's Crusade followers walked behind a goose they believed was holy.
Emperor Frederick II won Jerusalem in 1229 through a treaty, without a battle, while excommunicated.
King Richard the Lionheart was captured on the way home and ransomed for 150,000 marks.
Saladin reportedly sent Richard fruit and snow when he was sick (reported).
Frederick Barbarossa drowned in a river before reaching the Crusade.
The 'Children's Crusade' of 1212 is a mix of history and legend (legend).

wednesday.title: The Weirdest Medical Treatments in History
wednesday.subject: Historical medicine
wednesday.why: Gross-out comedy that stays PG, with a high share rate.
shorts: In the 1700s, London had kits by the Thames for blowing tobacco smoke into drowned people to revive them.
In 1898 Bayer sold heroin as a cough medicine.
Europeans ate powdered Egyptian mummy as medicine for centuries.
Doctors drained about 40% of George Washington's blood as treatment on the day he died in 1799.
Radium-laced water was sold as a health tonic in the 1920s.
The inventor of the lobotomy won a Nobel Prize in 1949.
Coca-Cola contained small amounts of cocaine until about 1903.

wednesday.title: The Craziest Things Hannibal Did
wednesday.subject: Hannibal Barca
wednesday.why: It follows the 'Craziest Things X Did' formula with the Rome audience, and elephants make it visual.
shorts: Hannibal marched war elephants over the Alps in 218 BC.
At age 9 he swore an oath to be Rome's enemy forever (Polybius).
He lost the sight in one eye marching through flooded marshes.
He escaped a Roman trap by driving cattle with burning torches on their horns at night.
At Cannae he encircled and destroyed a much larger Roman army in one afternoon.
In a naval battle he reportedly had pots of snakes thrown onto enemy ships (Cornelius Nepos).
He stayed undefeated in Italy for about 15 years but never besieged Rome itself.

wednesday.title: The Craziest Spies in History
wednesday.subject: Spies
wednesday.why: Espionage thriller energy that is safe and fun, with strong WWII interest.
shorts: Double agent 'Garbo' invented 27 fake sub-agents and got both a German Iron Cross and a British MBE.
Virginia Hall spied in occupied France with a prosthetic leg she named 'Cuthbert'.
Harriet Tubman led a Union raid in 1863 that freed about 750 enslaved people.
Agent Zigzag, Eddie Chapman, faked the bombing of an aircraft factory with painted canvas.
Josephine Baker smuggled secrets written in invisible ink on her sheet music (reported).
Mata Hari was executed as a spy in 1917, but historians doubt she gave the Germans much.
The Gestapo reportedly called Virginia Hall 'the most dangerous of all Allied spies'.
Playwright Christopher Marlowe may have worked for Queen Elizabeth I's spy network (debated).

wednesday.title: The Craziest Olympic Moments in History
wednesday.subject: Olympics
wednesday.why: Sports crossover pulls a broad audience. The 1904 marathon alone is a viral short.
shorts: In the 1904 Olympic marathon, Fred Lorz rode in a car for miles and briefly 'won'.
The 1904 marathon winner was fed strychnine and brandy by his trainers during the race.
Cuban runner Andarín Carvajal ran the 1904 marathon after stopping to eat rotten apples and nap.
The Olympics awarded medals for painting, music and literature from 1912 to 1948.
Tug-of-war was an Olympic sport from 1900 to 1920.
Ancient Olympic athletes competed naked.
The 1900 Paris Olympics included live pigeon shooting, the only time it was an Olympic event.
Married women were barred from even watching the ancient Olympic Games.

wednesday.title: The Most Insane Hoaxes in History
wednesday.subject: Hoaxes
wednesday.why: Fake-news-of-the-past is a very shareable and advertiser-safe angle.
shorts: In 1835 the New York Sun claimed astronomers had seen bat-people on the Moon.
In 1957 the BBC fooled viewers with a report on Swiss farmers harvesting spaghetti from trees.
The Piltdown Man 'missing link' fooled scientists from 1912 until 1953.
Two girls' 1917 Cottingley Fairies photos fooled Arthur Conan Doyle; they admitted the hoax in the 1980s.
In 1810 a prankster sent hundreds of tradesmen and dignitaries to one London address (Berners Street hoax).
When P.T. Barnum couldn't buy the fake Cardiff Giant, he made a fake of the fake.
The 1938 'War of the Worlds' mass panic was largely exaggerated by newspapers (legend).

wednesday.title: The Craziest Battles Won Against Impossible Odds
wednesday.subject: Last stands
wednesday.why: Serious History's 'Craziest Fights' did 1.1M and '1v1 Fights' 3.1M. Underdog stories get high retention.
shorts: At Saragarhi in 1897, 21 Sikh soldiers held a post against thousands of attackers.
At Rorke's Drift in 1879, about 150 British soldiers held off 3,000 to 4,000 Zulu warriors; 11 Victoria Crosses were awarded.
In 1945 American soldiers and anti-Nazi German soldiers fought side by side to defend Castle Itter.
Jack Churchill went into WWII with a longbow and a sword and played the bagpipes into battle.
At Agincourt in 1415 a smaller English army with longbows beat a much larger French force.
The '300 Spartans' at Thermopylae actually fought alongside several thousand other Greeks.
Jack Churchill is credited with the only recorded longbow kill of WWII.

wednesday.title: The Weirdest Laws in History
wednesday.subject: Laws
wednesday.why: Relatable and funny, easily visual, and brand-safe.
shorts: England taxed windows from 1696, so people bricked theirs up; you can still see blocked windows today.
Peter the Great made Russians pay a beard tax.
Massachusetts banned celebrating Christmas from 1659 to 1681.
Medieval Europe held trials for animals; a pig was executed in Falaise in 1386.
Rome taxed urine collected from public toilets.
England taxed hats from 1784 to 1811.
Ancient Rome had laws limiting who could wear purple.

wednesday.title: The Craziest Things Vikings Did
wednesday.subject: Vikings
wednesday.why: Vikings are evergreen, and this entry can sit with the Monday Vikings episode.
shorts: In 845 Vikings sailed up the Seine and were paid thousands of pounds of silver to leave Paris.
A Viking carved his name in runes on a balcony in the Hagia Sophia.
Harald Hardrada served in the Byzantine emperor's Varangian Guard before becoming king of Norway.
Huge hoards of Islamic silver coins found in Scandinavia show Vikings traded as far as the Middle East.
Vikings founded Dublin in the 840s.
Gudrid Thorbjarnardóttir travelled to North America and later made a pilgrimage to Rome.
The Paris raid being led by Ragnar Lothbrok is partly legendary (legend).

wednesday.title: The Weirdest Things Ancient Egyptians Did
wednesday.subject: Ancient Egypt
wednesday.why: Egypt is a top evergreen topic, and the weird-habits angle gets high share.
shorts: Egyptians tested pregnancy by peeing on wheat and barley; a 1963 test found it worked about 70% of the time.
Herodotus wrote that Egyptians shaved their eyebrows in mourning when the family cat died.
Egyptians mummified millions of animals, especially cats.
In 1890 a shipment of about 180,000 cat mummies was ground up as fertiliser in England.
Egyptian tomb workers were paid partly in beer.
Egyptian eye makeup (kohl) may have helped fight eye infections.
The story that Ramesses II's mummy got a passport in 1976 is widely repeated but unconfirmed (legend).

wednesday.title: The Worst Jobs in History
wednesday.subject: Jobs
wednesday.why: Relatable comedy that is highly visual.
shorts: The 'Groom of the Stool' helped Henry VIII on the toilet, and it was a powerful position.
'Gong farmers' dug out cesspits by hand at night in Tudor England.
Leech collectors waded into ponds and let leeches bite their legs.
Victorian 'toshers' searched London's sewers for coins.
'Knocker-uppers' woke workers by tapping on windows with long poles or pea shooters.
'Whipping boys' are said to have been punished instead of misbehaving princes (partly legend).
Welsh 'sin-eaters' supposedly ate bread over a corpse to absorb the dead person's sins (folk tradition, partly legend).

wednesday.title: The Most Bizarre Royal Habits in History
wednesday.subject: Royal habits
wednesday.why: Royals are high-interest, and the habits bring easy gags.
shorts: Louis XIV's waking-up routine (the lever) was a ceremony watched by courtiers.
Peter the Great collected the teeth he pulled from his courtiers.
Queen Victoria reportedly had Prince Albert's clothes laid out daily for decades after his death.
Philip V of Spain went through phases of refusing to cut his hair or nails.
Emperor Rudolf II kept a pet lion and a huge cabinet of curiosities in Prague.
Ludwig II of Bavaria took late-night sleigh rides in costume.
Henry VIII's 'Groom of the Stool' was one of the most trusted men at court.
Charles II walked his many spaniels through the palace so often that the breed is named after him.

wednesday.title: The Craziest Inventions and Weapons from History
wednesday.subject: Wacky inventions
wednesday.why: Visual gag heaven that is brand-safe.
shorts: In WWII, B.F. Skinner trained pigeons to steer missiles (Project Pigeon).
The US tested 'bat bombs': bats carrying tiny firebombs.
Britain built the Great Panjandrum, a rocket-powered wheel of explosives, and it went badly.
Britain planned an aircraft carrier made of ice and sawdust ('Pykrete').
In the 1930s some London mothers hung babies in cages outside apartment windows for fresh air.
Heron of Alexandria built a steam-powered spinning device in the 1st century AD.
Germany's WWII 'Gustav' railway gun weighed about 1,350 tonnes.

wednesday.title: The Most Advanced Ancient Technology
wednesday.subject: Ancient tech
wednesday.why: Mystery and awe that is safe and evergreen, a good closer for the list.
shorts: The Antikythera mechanism (about 100 BC) predicted eclipses with bronze gears.
Roman concrete contains lime chunks that can 'self-heal' cracks, according to a 2023 MIT study.
The Roman Lycurgus Cup changes colour in light thanks to tiny gold and silver particles.
Heron of Alexandria designed a coin-operated holy water dispenser.
Romans heated floors with 'hypocaust' underfloor heating.
The Byzantine recipe for Greek fire is lost.
The 'Baghdad Battery' being an ancient electric battery is disputed (legend).

friday.title: Mansa Musa: The Richest Man Who Ever Lived
friday.subject: Mansa Musa
friday.why: The richest-person hook plus finance RPM; TED-Ed's version has 8.9M views. A fresh cartoon take is proven.
shorts: Mansa Musa's 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca reportedly travelled with thousands of people and camels loaded with gold.
He gave away so much gold in Cairo that its value there stayed depressed for about 12 years (al-Umari).
He reportedly had to borrow money back at high interest before leaving Cairo.
The 1375 Catalan Atlas shows him on a throne holding a gold nugget.
He brought back an architect who helped build Timbuktu's Djinguereber mosque.
Mali supplied a large share of the gold used in the Mediterranean world.
Modern '$400 billion' net worth numbers are guesses; his wealth can't really be measured.
Claims that he built a mosque every Friday on the journey are legend (legend).

friday.title: The Richest People in History (Ranked)
friday.subject: Richest people
friday.why: The list format plus money plus finance RPM, with huge evergreen search.
shorts: Augustus personally owned Egypt, the empire's richest province.
Crassus said no one was truly rich unless they could fund an army from their own income (Plutarch).
A 2007 study estimated Norman lord Alan Rufus held about 7% of England's national income.
Jakob Fugger lent most of the money used to bribe the electors who chose Charles V as emperor in 1519.
John D. Rockefeller is often called America's first billionaire (around 1916).
The Nizam of Hyderabad, on Time's cover as the world's richest man in 1937, used a 185-carat diamond as a paperweight.
Andrew Carnegie sold his steel company for $480 million in 1901.

friday.title: The Biggest Heists in History
friday.subject: Heists
friday.why: Heists are proven clickbait; 'The Dumbest Heist in History' performs, and money topics bring higher RPM.
shorts: The Mona Lisa was stolen in 1911 by a museum worker who hid inside the Louvre, and it wasn't recovered until 1913.
In 1671 Colonel Blood stole the Crown Jewels, flattened the crown with a mallet, and was pardoned by Charles II.
The 1983 Brink's-Mat robbers expected about £3 million in cash and found £26 million in gold.
The 2003 Antwerp diamond thieves were caught partly thanks to a half-eaten salami sandwich.
Ireland's Crown Jewels vanished from Dublin Castle in 1907 and have never been found.
Thieves dressed as police stole 13 artworks from Boston's Gardner Museum in 1990; the frames still hang empty.
The 1963 Great Train Robbery took about £2.6 million.

friday.title: The Greatest Con Artists in History
friday.subject: Scams
friday.why: Scams equal money and drama; Serious History 'Craziest Scams in Ancient Civilizations' 468K.
shorts: Victor Lustig 'sold' the Eiffel Tower for scrap to a dealer in 1925, then reportedly tried again.
Gregor MacGregor sold land and bonds in 'Poyais', a country that did not exist.
Charles Ponzi promised 50% returns in 45 days in 1920 and gave his name to the Ponzi scheme.
Thérèse Humbert borrowed fortunes against a locked safe; when it was opened in 1902 it held almost nothing.
Cassie Chadwick pretended to be Andrew Carnegie's secret daughter and borrowed millions.
George C. Parker reportedly 'sold' the Brooklyn Bridge to tourists more than once (reported).
Many of Frank Abagnale's 'Catch Me If You Can' claims have been challenged (partly legend).

friday.title: Tulip Mania: The Craziest Market Bubble in History
friday.subject: Tulip Mania
friday.why: The famous first bubble, a finance keyword magnet with high RPM.
shorts: At the peak in 1637, a single rare tulip bulb reportedly cost as much as a fine Amsterdam house.
The prized striped 'broken' tulips were actually caused by a plant virus.
Bulbs were traded as futures in taverns long before they were dug up.
The crash began in February 1637 when buyers stopped showing up at an auction in Haarlem.
Modern historians think far fewer people were ruined than the legend says.
The sailor who ate a priceless tulip bulb thinking it was an onion is a legend (legend).
Tulips originally came to the Netherlands from the Ottoman Empire.

friday.title: Crassus: The Richest Man in Rome and His Humiliating Death
friday.subject: Crassus
friday.why: Serious History's 'HUMILIATING Death of the Richest Man in Rome' got 1.2M. It combines money, power and Rome.
shorts: Crassus ran a private fire brigade that bought burning buildings cheap before putting the fire out (Plutarch).
He guaranteed Julius Caesar's huge debts, helping launch Caesar's career.
He crushed Spartacus's slave revolt in 71 BC.
He formed the First Triumvirate with Caesar and Pompey.
At 60 he marched into the desert chasing glory and lost at Carrhae in 53 BC.
Molten gold being poured down his throat is a later story (legend).
Crassus owned silver mines and bought up property seized from Sulla's political enemies cheaply.

friday.title: The Worst Hyperinflations in History
friday.subject: Hyperinflation
friday.why: Money plus shocking visuals (wheelbarrows of cash); a timeless finance search.
shorts: In November 1923 one US dollar was worth about 4.2 trillion German marks.
Germans used cash as wallpaper and kids played with bundles of money because it was cheaper.
In 1946 prices in Hungary doubled roughly every 15 hours, the worst hyperinflation ever recorded.
Hungary printed a 100 quintillion pengő note.
Zimbabwe issued a 100 trillion dollar note in 2009.
Germany's new Rentenmark replaced 1 trillion old paper marks.
Rome's silver coin fell from mostly silver to only a few percent silver in the 3rd century.

friday.title: John D. Rockefeller: The Richest American Ever
friday.subject: Rockefeller
friday.why: Rockefeller is a top business-history figure with strong US tier-1 RPM.
shorts: At his peak Rockefeller's fortune equalled roughly 1.5% of the entire US economy.
By about 1880 Standard Oil controlled around 90% of US oil refining.
In 1911 the Supreme Court broke Standard Oil into 34 companies, ancestors of ExxonMobil and Chevron.
He tracked every cent he spent from age 16 in a notebook he called 'Ledger A'.
In old age he handed out dimes to people he met.
The breakup made him even richer, because shares in the new companies soared.
Rockefeller lived to 97 and gave away over $500 million in his lifetime.

friday.title: The Wall Street Crash of 1929 Explained
friday.subject: 1929 Crash
friday.why: A finance keyword powerhouse with the highest RPM potential of any history topic.
shorts: On Black Tuesday, October 29, 1929, about 16 million shares changed hands.
The Dow did not regain its 1929 peak until 1954.
Many buyers used margin, putting down as little as 10% and borrowing the rest.
Days before the crash, economist Irving Fisher said stocks had reached a 'permanently high plateau'.
Winston Churchill was in New York during the crash.
The wave of bankers jumping out of windows is mostly a myth (legend).
Joseph Kennedy selling after a shoeshine boy gave him stock tips is an anecdote (legend).

friday.title: The Medici: The Bankers Who Bought the Pope
friday.subject: Medici
friday.why: Money, power and the Renaissance, with high RPM and TV-show awareness.
shorts: The Medici family produced four popes.
In 1478 rivals attacked the Medici brothers during Mass; Giuliano was killed and Lorenzo escaped.
Galileo named Jupiter's moons the 'Medicean Stars' to win the Medici's patronage.
Catherine de' Medici became Queen of France.
The last Medici, Anna Maria Luisa, left the family's art to Florence on condition that it never leave the city.
The Medici Bank collapsed in 1494.
The claim that Catherine de' Medici brought the fork to France is a legend (legend).

friday.title: The South Sea Bubble: How Isaac Newton Lost a Fortune
friday.subject: South Sea and Mississippi bubbles
friday.why: A famous-genius-goes-broke hook with finance RPM.
shorts: South Sea Company shares rose from about £128 to around £1,000 in 1720, then crashed.
Isaac Newton reportedly lost around £20,000 in the bubble.
John Law, a Scot who had escaped prison after killing a man in a duel, ended up running France's finances.
Law's Mississippi Company mania in Paris helped popularise the word 'millionaire'.
Britain passed the Bubble Act in 1720 to ban unauthorised companies.
The 'company for carrying on an undertaking of great advantage, but nobody to know what it is' may be apocryphal (legend).
Newton's quote about the 'madness of people' is attributed to him but not verified (legend).

friday.title: The Dutch East India Company: The Most Powerful Company Ever
friday.subject: VOC
friday.why: The first-stock-market hook plus a company-with-an-army story; finance RPM.
shorts: The Dutch East India Company (1602) was the first company to sell shares to the public.
It could raise armies, wage war, mint coins and sign treaties.
In 1667 the Dutch kept the tiny nutmeg island of Run and let England keep Manhattan.
Amsterdam's stock exchange grew up around trading its shares.
It paid dividends for close to two centuries before being dissolved in 1799.
Nutmeg was so valuable in Europe that it was worth fighting wars over.
The VOC founded Cape Town in 1652 as a supply station for its ships.

friday.title: How Pirates Actually Made Money
friday.subject: Pirate economics
friday.why: Pirates plus economics is a fun money explainer with broad appeal.
shorts: In 1695 Henry Every robbed the Mughal treasure ship Ganj-i-Sawai, one of the richest pirate hauls ever, and was never caught.
Pirate crews voted for their captains and split loot by written shares.
Pirate articles paid fixed compensation for lost limbs.
Captain Kidd really did bury treasure on Gardiners Island, New York; it was dug up in 1699.
Blackbeard's flagship wreck was found off North Carolina in 1996.
Buried pirate treasure maps with an 'X' are mostly fiction (legend).
Spanish 'pieces of eight' were the coin pirates wanted most; they were used worldwide.

friday.title: The Weirdest Money in History
friday.subject: Strange currencies
friday.why: A curiosity plus finance angle that yields very short-able facts.
shorts: On Yap, giant stone discs called rai were money, and ownership changed without moving the stones.
Aztecs used cacao beans as money; a 1545 list priced a turkey hen at 100 beans.
In 1685 French Canada paid soldiers with playing cards signed as money.
Medieval England used notched 'tally sticks' as records; burning old ones in 1834 set Parliament on fire.
Ancient China used bronze coins shaped like knives.
Cigarettes served as currency in WWII prison camps.
In medieval Russia, animal pelts such as marten were used as money.

friday.title: How the Spanish Empire Went Broke (With All the Silver in the World)
friday.subject: Spanish silver
friday.why: An irony hook (richest empire, broke), with economics RPM.
shorts: Potosí's silver mountain was so rich that 'vale un Potosí' means 'worth a fortune' in Spanish.
Philip II defaulted on his debts four times despite the silver.
Spanish silver dollars were legal tender in the USA until 1857.
The Manila galleons carried silver across the Pacific to China for 250 years.
So much silver flooded Europe that it helped cause a long 'price revolution' of inflation.
Atahualpa offered to fill a room once with gold and twice with silver to buy his freedom.
Spain's King Charles V borrowed so heavily from the Fugger bank that Spanish silver often went straight to foreign creditors.

friday.title: How the Roman Empire Made (and Lost) Its Money
friday.subject: Roman economy
friday.why: Rome's audience plus economics; it links to the Monday Rome video.
shorts: The Roman silver denarius was debased until coins held only a few percent silver.
In 301 AD Diocletian tried to fix prices for over 1,000 goods by law, and it failed.
Rome gave free grain to about 200,000 citizens.
Rome outsourced tax collection to private 'publicani', who often squeezed provinces hard.
A gold coin celebrating Caesar's assassination ('EID MAR') sold for about $4 million in 2020.
The idea that Roman soldiers were paid in salt (giving us 'salary') is debated (legend).
Emperor Vespasian taxed urine collected from public toilets: 'money doesn't stink'.

friday.title: The Gold Rush: Who Actually Got Rich?
friday.subject: California Gold Rush
friday.why: A US-centric, high-RPM topic with a surprising 'the shovel sellers won' twist.
shorts: Sam Brannan reportedly ran through San Francisco shouting 'Gold!' after buying up all the shovels and pans to resell.
John Sutter, on whose land gold was found in 1848, ended up broke.
San Francisco grew from about 1,000 people to about 25,000 in a year.
Hundreds of ships were abandoned in San Francisco harbour as crews ran to the gold fields; some became buildings.
Levi Strauss and Jacob Davis patented riveted work pants in 1873.
Prices skyrocketed, and eggs reportedly sold for up to $1 each.
The Gold Rush began when James Marshall found gold at Sutter's Mill on January 24, 1848.

friday.title: The Most Expensive Mistakes in History
friday.subject: Costly blunders
friday.why: Money plus facepalm makes a strong hybrid of the Wednesday and Friday formats.
shorts: Russia sold Alaska for $7.2 million in 1867, about 2 cents an acre.
NASA lost the $125 million Mars Climate Orbiter in 1999 because of a metric vs imperial unit mix-up.
Napoleon sold the Louisiana territory to the USA for about $15 million.
Scotland's Darien scheme lost a huge share of the nation's wealth.
Apple co-founder Ronald Wayne sold his 10% stake for $800 in 1976.
Decca's 'guitar groups are on the way out' line when rejecting the Beatles is likely embellished (legend).
The Spanish Armada of 1588 lost around a third of its ships, many to storms off Scotland and Ireland.

friday.title: Jakob Fugger: The Banker Who Bought an Emperor
friday.subject: Jakob Fugger
friday.why: An under-covered richest-man topic with high RPM.
shorts: Jakob Fugger supplied most of the bribe money that got Charles V elected emperor in 1519.
He later reminded the emperor in writing that he would not have the crown without Fugger's help.
He founded the Fuggerei in 1516, the world's oldest social housing still in use.
Fuggerei rent is still 0.88 euro a year plus daily prayers.
His loans to an archbishop were repaid through indulgence sales, the trade Martin Luther attacked.
He built his fortune on silver and copper mining.
Fugger even wrote his own epitaph, describing himself as second to none in wealth.

friday.title: The Darien Scheme: How Scotland Went Bankrupt
friday.subject: Darien scheme
friday.why: A little-known shocking story with UK tier-1 appeal.
shorts: In 1698 Scotland tried to found a trading colony in Panama called New Caledonia.
Scots invested a huge share of the nation's available capital.
Colonists brought wool clothing and wigs to trade in the tropics.
Disease, Spanish attacks and an English trade boycott destroyed the colony.
Most of the settlers died or fled.
The 1707 union with England included a payment called 'the Equivalent', partly to cover Darien losses.
The Company of Scotland raised about £400,000, a vast sum for Scotland then.

friday.title: The British East India Company: The Corporation That Conquered India
friday.subject: British East India Company
friday.why: Corporate-power history with finance and business RPM. Keep it framed neutrally.
shorts: The East India Company began with a royal charter on December 31, 1600.
By 1803 it had a private army of about 260,000, roughly twice the size of the British Army.
The tea dumped in the Boston Tea Party belonged to the East India Company.
The English word 'loot' comes from Hindi.
The British government had to bail the company out in 1772.
It was dissolved in 1874.
The Company's trade in opium to China helped trigger the Opium Wars.

friday.title: Andrew Carnegie: From $1.20 a Week to Richest Man in the World
friday.subject: Andrew Carnegie
friday.why: Rags-to-riches plus finance; motivational crossover.
shorts: Carnegie's first job at 13 paid $1.20 a week as a bobbin boy.
He sold Carnegie Steel to J.P. Morgan for $480 million in 1901.
He paid for 2,509 libraries around the world.
He wrote that 'the man who dies thus rich dies disgraced'.
He paid for Carnegie Hall, which opened in 1891.
He gave away about 90% of his fortune.
Carnegie arrived in the US at age 12 as a poor Scottish immigrant.

friday.title: J.P. Morgan: The Man Who Bailed Out America Twice
friday.subject: J.P. Morgan
friday.why: Banking history with high finance RPM.
shorts: In 1895 J.P. Morgan helped rescue the US Treasury's gold reserve.
In the Panic of 1907 he locked bankers in his library until they agreed to a rescue.
His US Steel (1901) was the first billion-dollar corporation.
He booked a suite on the Titanic but cancelled.
The 1907 panic led to the creation of the Federal Reserve in 1913.
Rockefeller reportedly said of Morgan's estate, 'and he wasn't even a rich man' (legend).
Morgan was so self-conscious about his swollen nose that he disliked being photographed.

friday.title: The Knights Templar: The Medieval Bank That Got Destroyed
friday.subject: Knights Templar
friday.why: Mystery plus money, with evergreen Templar search demand.
shorts: Templars let pilgrims deposit money in Europe and withdraw it in the Holy Land, an early traveller's cheque.
King Philip IV of France owed them money and had them arrested on October 13, 1307.
Richard the Lionheart sold Cyprus to the Templars, who soon gave it back.
Their last Grand Master, Jacques de Molay, was burned in 1314; the king and the pope both died within the year.
The link between Friday the 13th superstition and the Templars is a modern myth (legend).
Lost Templar treasure is legend (legend).
The Templars started around 1119 as a small band of knights guarding pilgrims.

friday.title: The Silk Road: The Richest Trade Route in History
friday.subject: Silk Road
friday.why: Economics plus Asia/Europe gives broad global appeal.
shorts: The term 'Silk Road' was coined in 1877 by a German geographer.
Pliny complained that Rome spent 100 million sesterces a year on luxuries from India, China and Arabia.
Rome's Senate tried to ban men from wearing silk.
Monks smuggled silkworm eggs to Byzantium around 552.
Marco Polo was amazed that China used paper money.
Sogdian merchants from Central Asia were key middlemen of the route.
The Silk Road also carried paper, gunpowder and ideas west from China.

friday.title: The Richest Kingdoms in African History
friday.subject: African wealth
friday.why: An under-served, growing audience that pairs with Mansa Musa.
shorts: An 11th-century writer said the King of Ghana's dogs wore gold collars (al-Bakri, reported).
Great Zimbabwe's massive stone walls were built without mortar.
The Kingdom of Aksum minted its own gold coins.
A small gold rhinoceros from Mapungubwe (about 13th century) is a South African national treasure.
Kilwa on the Swahili coast minted its own coins and traded as far as China.
Mali controlled some of the richest gold fields of the medieval world.
Trans-Saharan caravans traded salt south and gold north across the desert.

friday.title: How Ancient Egypt Became the Richest Kingdom on Earth
friday.subject: Egyptian wealth
friday.why: Egypt demand plus money; the Tut gold visual.
shorts: Tutankhamun's inner coffin is made of about 110 kg of solid gold.
A foreign king wrote to Pharaoh that in Egypt 'gold is as plentiful as dust' (Amarna letters).
Egypt set taxes by measuring the Nile flood with 'nilometers'.
Workers were paid in grain and beer.
Papyri record trials of tomb robbers around 1110 BC.
Under Rome, Egypt's grain helped feed the capital.
Egypt controlled rich gold mines in Nubia, whose name may relate to the Egyptian word for gold, 'nub' (debated).
